We have said this before in the story of the mother of Musa, when God said to her: ﴿And when you fear for him, cast him into the river, and do not fear and do not grieve...﴾ [al-Qasas: 7]. Consider: would she accept, or fear for her child that she would cast him into the sea?

Would she accept to save him from a supposed death by a certain death? But she believed, affirmed, and carried out the command. Because God turned her heart, and the inspiration of the Merciful is not opposed or thwarted by the inspiration of Satan. Therefore He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And know that God intervenes between a person and his heart...﴾ [al-Anfal: 24].

This matter also happened with Pharaoh. God intervened between him and his heart and what he wanted. He was searching for children and killing them, yet a child came to him in a chest cast upon the river, in a suspicious form that invites doubt, and still he received him, embraced him, raised him, and believed his wife when she said about the boy: ﴿A comfort of the eye for me and for you...﴾ [al-Qasas: 9].

So: this is stupidity, from whom? From Pharaoh, who claimed divinity and said to the people: "I am your lord, the Most High."

Then, when we reflect on the story, we find other indications of this man's foolishness. The magicians told him that the end of his kingdom would come at the hand of a boy born among the Children of Israel. Since you have believed this prophecy, why do you kill the children?

So: God's decrees must come to pass, and their causes are prepared for them. This is the meaning of ﴿While they both call upon God for help...﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 17]: they are saying, "O Lord, You are capable of everything and You are above causes. We have no stratagem with this son, and it grieves us to leave him in disbelief so that he perishes."

Our master, the Messenger of God (ﷺ), taught us to turn to God. Whenever a matter overwhelmed him, that is, overpowered him and its causes became constricted, he would stand in prayer to stand before his Lord, and He would loosen for him every hardship and ease every difficulty.

The word ﴿Believe﴾ (آمِنْ) means: utter the testimony and acknowledge that God is one God. The root (a-m-n) has various meanings in the Qur'an. You say: "I believed in God" (āmantu billah). This verb takes the preposition "bi," meaning: I testified and affirmed. And "āmantu lahu" means: I affirmed him as truthful, as in His saying: ﴿But you will not be believed by us...﴾ [Yusuf: 17], meaning: you will not be trusted as truthful. And "āmantuhu" means: I gave him security.

Their saying: ﴿Indeed, the promise of God is true...﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 17] confirms this reality to him. Since it is true, it will happen and there is no escape from it, because God is one God with no partner, and no one can annul or oppose this promise, and He is the Mighty and Powerful who has the ability to carry out what He has promised.

Therefore, concerning the Hour, He said: ﴿The command of God has come, so do not seek to hasten it. Glory be to Him and exalted is He above what they associate with Him﴾ [al-Nahl: 1]. Here it is in the past tense, because God's promise encompasses the past, present and future alike. He, glorified is He, is the Creator of time, its Owner, and the One who disposes of it. So He expresses the future in the past tense because He knows that no power can oppose it.

So: the Resurrection that will come in the future has in fact come, and it is an event beyond doubt. Therefore He acts in the universe by His own testimony, glorified is He. The first to believe was God Himself in His own essence, so He said: ﴿God bears witness that there is no god but Him...﴾ [Al 'Imran: 18].

God bore witness to His own essence before any of His creatures bore witness to it. It is as if, glorified is He, by this testimony He commits Himself to everything He wills, knowing that it will not fail. And it is only "Be, and it is."

Likewise our master, the Messenger of God, bore witness to his own prophethood before anyone bore witness to it. So in a narration—

So His saying: ﴿Indeed, the promise of God is true...﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 17] means: truthful and not failing. The truth is the thing that is established and does not change, because God is the One who decreed it and judged it, so no one changes it. Therefore He, glorified is He, says: ﴿The way of God that has already passed before, and you will not find any change in the way of God﴾ [al-Fath: 23].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And he says, "This is nothing but the fables of the former peoples"﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 17].

That is: this stubborn son says to his parents, while they are calling him to belief in the Resurrection and the rising again: "What you are saying is nothing but the fables of the ancients," meaning their lies and stories that came in their books. That is, what you call me to is a falsehood resembling fables and superstitions.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 46, verse 18:

We notice that the discussion in the previous verse was about a singular figure, the one who said to his parents, ﴿Uff to you both!﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 17]. Here, however, Allah the Exalted refers to him in the plural form ﴿Those are...﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 18], so He brings the verdict and speaks of him in the plural: ﴿Those are the ones against whom the Word has been justified...﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 18].

It is as if (alladhi, "the one who") is understood not as singular but as plural, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿By time! Indeed, mankind is in loss, except for those who believe...﴾ [al-Asr: 1-3], where He made an exception of the plural from the singular.

They said about this verse what they said about the previous verse, namely that it was revealed concerning ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr. But this view does not fit the meaning of the verse, because our master ʿAbd al-Rahman embraced Islam and his Islam was good, whereas this verse speaks of those against whom the punishment has been decreed. Therefore it was revealed concerning another person, not ʿAbd al-Rahman.

A story about this matter appears in the history books. The one who said that the verse was revealed concerning ʿAbd al-Rahman was Marwan ibn al-Hakam, who was governor of Madinah.

When Muʿawiyah gave the pledge of allegiance to his son Yazid as caliph, he asked Marwan to take the pledge of allegiance for Yazid. ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr objected to this.

He said: "Have you made it Heraclian (hirqliyyah)? That is, a monarchy in which the son succeeds his father?" Marwan said: "Be quiet, you!" Then he said: "Do you know who this is? This is the one about whom Allah said, ﴿But the one who said to his parents, 'Uff to you both!'﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 17]."

When this statement reached our mother ʿAʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, she said: "By Allah, it is not him. Had I wished to name the one about whom it was said, I would have named him. But say to Marwan: Allah has cursed you in the loins of your father."

This is because al-Hakam ibn al-ʿAs once used to imitate the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in his walk, mocking him. The Prophet (ﷺ) turned and saw him, and gestured to him with his hand, so he was banished to al-Ta'if. After the honour he had enjoyed in Madinah, he became a shepherd of sheep, until our master ʿUthman came and interceded for him with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he was permitted to return.

However, the Companions said: "We did not hear this from the Messenger." ʿUthman said: "I heard it from him."

The meaning of ﴿the Word has been justified against them...﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 18] is: the punishment that We warned them of has become due and certain for them, ﴿among nations that passed away before them...﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 18], meaning, went away and departed, ﴿of jinn and humankind. Indeed, they were losers﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 18], because Allah said of the believers, ﴿The believers have certainly succeeded﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1].

So, in contrast, the disbelieving deniers have lost.

This verse indicates that the jinn too are accountable, and among them are the obedient and the disobedient, the believer and the disbeliever. For this reason He said in Surah al-Jinn, ﴿As for the deviators, they have become fuel for Hell﴾ [al-Jinn: 15]. Thus they will be punished in a manner suited to their nature.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 46, verse 19:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And for each﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 19]: for each of the two categories: the believers, mentioned earlier in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remain steadfast...﴾ [Fussilat: 30], and the disbelievers, about whom Allah said: ﴿Those are the ones upon whom the word has been justified...﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 18].

So for each of the believer and the disbeliever, the obedient and the disobedient, there is a recompense according to the measure of his rank and station: ﴿there are degrees for what they have done...﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 19].

It is well known that Paradise has degrees (darajat), and that the Fire, may Allah protect us, has levels of descent (darakat). For this reason Allah said: ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest level of the Fire...﴾ [al-Nisa': 145]. But here He made them "degrees" for both the believers and the disbelievers. How so?

They said: this is a kind of mockery, ridicule and rebuke directed at them, as in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿So give them tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 24].

It is well known that punishment is not given as glad tidings; glad tidings are only given of something pleasant and joyful. Therefore, this is sarcasm, as in ﴿Taste! Indeed, you are the mighty, the noble﴾ [al-Dukhan: 49], and he is in this situation humiliated, tormented and despised. Or: He calls them "degrees" in order to enrage them, so that they increase in regret and pain.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And that He may fully pay them their deeds﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 19] is from wafa' (fulfilment), which is that you give the recompense in full without deficiency, as you say: "I paid so-and-so his debt" (wafaytu fulanan dinahu), meaning: I gave him in full. ﴿And they will not be wronged﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 19], meaning: they will not have anything reduced from their rewards.

The purpose here: the grammatical estimate is: "Mention, O Muhammad, the Day when those who disbelieve are exposed to the Fire." When you see a time-frame (zarf), look for the event within it, because time is not praised or blamed in itself; it is judged by the action that takes place in it.

The event here is that those who disbelieve are exposed to the Fire. But who is exposed to whom? The Fire is not rational and the disbelievers are rational. The Fire is exposed to them, as you say: "I displayed the cloth to the buyer." But on the Day of Resurrection it will become clear to them that the Fire is rational, and that they are the ones who will be exposed to it.

Recite: ﴿On the Day We say to Hell, "Are you filled?" and it says, "Are there any more?"﴾ [Qaf: 30]. It is established in the noble hadith that it longs for its people among the disbelievers and the disobedient, and that it will speak and utter words.

Allah, glorified is He, addresses whomever He wills in whatever manner He wills. Therefore we do not understand this verse by the laws of human beings, for God has other laws concerning things. So if He teaches any of His creatures something of them, that person will know it and deal with it accordingly, as we see in the story of our master Solomon, peace be upon him: ﴿So We gave Solomon understanding of it...﴾ [al-Anbiya: 79].

He understood the language of animals and birds. So when he heard the ant and understood what it said, he smiled laughing at her words, and he thanked the One who had bestowed this blessing upon him.

Some have said that there is an inversion (qalb) in the verse, as you say: "I presented the trough to the she-camel," whereas in reality you present the she-camel to the trough so that it may drink from it.

And the saying of the Exalted: ﴿You squandered your good things in your worldly life and enjoyed them...﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 20] means: this speech is addressed to them in the Hereafter, after the Hour has been established. But there is another verse that some think contradicts this one.

It is His saying: ﴿The Fire; they are exposed to it morning and evening, and on the Day the Hour is established: "Admit the people of Pharaoh to the most severe punishment."﴾ [Ghafir: 46]. They understood from it that the exposure happens in this world, because the phrase "and on the Day the Hour is established" is joined to it by conjunction.

But one who reflects on this verse finds that this exposure is neither in this world nor in the Hereafter, but in the stage of the barzakh (the intermediate realm between death and resurrection). How so? Because the morning and evening (ghuduww and ʿashiyy) arise from the movement of the sun and the existence of night and day, and there is nothing of this in the Hereafter.

In the Hereafter there is no sun or moon, no night or day: ﴿The Day the earth will be replaced by other than the earth, and the heavens...﴾ [Ibrahim: 48]. In this world we live through causes, but in the Hereafter we live through the One who causes, glorified is He. The sun gives us light in this world, but in the Hereafter ﴿the earth will shine with the light of its Lord...﴾ [al-Zumar: 69].

So: the exposure here is in the barzakh. ﴿and on the Day the Hour is established: "Admit the people of Pharaoh to the most severe punishment."﴾ So the exposure is not in the Hereafter; rather it is the entering. The exposure in the first stage is different from the exposure in the second. And what tells you that before they enter the Fire they are not exposed to it? Because the Sirat is laid over the back of Hell, so they are exposed to the Fire before they enter it.

And the saying of the Exalted: ﴿You squandered your good things in your worldly life and enjoyed them...﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 20]. This verse has resolved a difficulty for us, since we see the people of disbelief and atheism having more wealth and adornment in this world than we do. Some ask about inventors and discoverers from among non-Muslims who served humanity with their knowledge: do they have a reward for that?

The answer is here: ﴿You squandered your good things in your worldly life...﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 20], and they have no share left in the Hereafter. This is the sunnah of Allah which does not change. Allah, exalted is He, gave the means to believers and to disbelievers alike.

Whoever excels in the means does not lose the fruit of his excellence, even if he is a disbeliever; and whoever sits back and neglects, is deprived, even if he is a believer, because this is the gift of lordship (rububiyyah).

As for those who offered this gift to humanity and served it with this service, was Allah in their minds? Never. What was in their minds was civilization, progress, serving history and humanity. They took their reward from it in fame, renown and the immortalizing of their memory: they erected statues for them and authored books about them.

So: they received their wages from those who worked for them, and the matter ended.

Therefore the Exalted says in describing the state of these people: ﴿And those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a level plain, which the thirsty one thinks is water, until, when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing; and he finds Allah with him, and He pays him in full his account. And Allah is swift in account.﴾ [al-Nur: 39].

He is confronted with a God who calls him to account, whom he had not had in mind at the hour of his work. This is the state of the disbeliever. As for the believer, he works in this world while his eye is on the Hereafter.

Our master ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz, before the caliphate, was well known as the pampered youth who lived in luxury night and day; he even wore silk. The servants who washed his clothes would take bribes from people so that they could wash their clothes in the water in which ʿUmar's garments had been washed, because of the abundance of perfume and fragrance in them.

When he assumed the caliphate, he renounced this luxury and lived a life of asceticism and austerity, and wore coarse garments. When they asked him about that, he said: "By Allah, if I wished, I would be the best of you in food and the finest of you in clothing, but I preserve my good things for the Hereafter. Indeed I have a soul that aspires — meaning: it has ambition for what is better. It longed for the emirate, and when it attained it, it longed for the caliphate, and when it attained it, it longed for Paradise."

Therefore it is narrated from our mother ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that she said: "The crescent would pass, then another crescent, then another crescent — meaning: three months would pass without fire being kindled in the house of Muhammad (ﷺ)." It was said: "Then what was your food?" She said: "The two blacks: water and dates."

However, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had neighbours from the Ansar who had milch animals, and they would give the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) some of their milk, and he would give us to drink. So the house of our master the Messenger of Allah was a model, an example, and a pattern for the poor.

And the saying: ﴿in your worldly life...﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 20]. By Allah, when you reflect on the meaning of the word "dunya" (the world/lower), do you find a description of it that is lower and less than this? And when you hear "dunya," you must remember its counterpart: that there is another life described as "the higher" (al-ʿulya), and it is the one in which the recompense is.

﴿So today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation...﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 20]: meaning, on the Day of Resurrection you will be repaid for your deeds with the punishment of humiliation (al-hawn), meaning: abasement and lowliness, because you were arrogant in the world in refusing the truth.

From this root (hawn) the word "hawn" is taken, which is the implement in the kitchen in which we pound things. It is the instrument of grinding, pounding and crushing the substance placed in it.

So it is as if the punishment they will encounter will crush their pride and make them humiliated and abased: ﴿because you were arrogant...﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 20], meaning: because of your arrogance and haughtiness in refusing the truth, ﴿in the land without right...﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 20]. This shows that there is a justified arrogance, which is that you be arrogant toward the arrogant. Therefore it was said: "Arrogance toward the arrogant is charity."

Thus our master Hamzah, in war, would wear the "headband of death," which is a red headband, and raise his sword, then walk between the ranks swaggering in self-admiration. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) looked at him and said: "This is a gait Allah dislikes, except in this situation," and he said: "May Allah have mercy on a man who displays strength to them from himself."

From the verses of the Noble Qur'an we understand that the believer, as described in the Qur'an, is not stamped with one nature or one mould; rather, the situation he is in dictates the nature suited to that situation.

Recite: ﴿Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and those with him are severe against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves...﴾ [al-Fath: 29], and He says: ﴿humble toward the believers, mighty against the disbelievers...﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 54].

So he is mighty in one situation and humble in another, severe in one situation and merciful in another. He combines two opposites, because the context differs.

And His saying: ﴿and because you were defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 20]. So there is arrogance and there is fisq (defiant disobedience). Arrogance is haughtiness in refusing the truth; fisq is from the expression "fasaqat al-ruṭbah," meaning: the date came out of its skin.

The date (balah) has stages in its ripening. When its size is complete, its colour begins to turn red or yellow, then it softens and gets a skin. If it is in a dry environment, it hardens and dries, and the skin sticks to the flesh of the date, and this is the finest kind of date.

So the meaning of fisq here is leaving the vessel of obedience. And when you reflect on arrogance and fisq, you find that they combine the work of the heart and the work of the limbs.

A human being has a heart and a body. The heart is the place of secrets and unseen matters, the place of sincerity or showing off, and the place of humility or haughtiness. So arrogance is an act of the heart. The Exalted said: ﴿and they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them, out of injustice and arrogance...﴾ [al-Naml: 14].

As for fisq, it is leaving obedience, which is the work of the limbs.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 46, verse 21:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And remember...﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 21]. That is: remember, O Muhammad. It is as if this remembrance came to remind the Messenger of the Prophet (ﷺ) of the stances of his brothers among the messengers in the procession of faith. That is: look at those before you among them and at what they bore in the cause of their call, for you are not an innovation among the messengers.

Indeed, they bore hardship and harm, but Allah fulfilled His promise to support them in the end. Therefore you notice in the style of the Qur'an the repetition of a single story through the multiplicity of events that pass over the Messenger. He, the Exalted, says: ﴿And We relate to you the news of the messengers, by which We strengthen your heart...﴾ [Hud: 120].

So whenever a matter befell the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with his people, Allah would remind him of a stance of the earlier messengers to reassure him and to make his heart firm upon the truth. And if every messenger was exposed to harm in proportion to his mission, then there is no doubt that you will be the most harmed of the messengers, because you are the Seal of the Prophets.

As for His saying: ﴿the brother of 'Ad...﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 21], what is meant is our master Hud. ﴿And to 'Ad their brother Hud...﴾ [al-A'raf: 65]. The word akh (brother) is pluralized as ikhwah and ikhwan. Ikhwah means brotherhood by lineage, as in His saying: ﴿And the brothers of Joseph came...﴾ [Yusuf: 58].

As for ikhwan, it is used to mean brotherhood of method, religion and values, as in His saying: ﴿Brothers, on couches facing one another﴾ [al-Hijr: 47]. So His saying ﴿the brother of 'Ad...﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 21] means their brother in lineage, and 'Ad is the tribe or the nation to which our master Hud, peace be upon him, was sent.

The idafah (annexation) in ﴿the brother of 'Ad...﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 21] is an appeal to their tenderness and an stirring of feelings of mercy, kinship and unity. The one who came to them is not a stranger to them; rather he is a brother to them, even if a method contrary to what they were upon came to them, and he wished to bring them out of the misguidance and corruption they had become accustomed to. A brother does not deceive his brother, whether their brotherhood to him is by lineage or by religion, method and values.

Therefore: they should receive his call with the tenderness that brotherhood requires.

﴿the brother of 'Ad, when he warned his people in al-Ahqaf...﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 21]. 'Ad was a group of the extinct Arabs, and they dwelt in al-Ahqaf in the south of the Arabian Peninsula. Al-Ahqaf is the plural of haqf: the elongated sand dune that rises and falls and moves to the right and to the left, here and there.

Because sand is soft, winds and hurricanes move it easily, to the extent that a single gust of a hurricane in this place would bury and cover a caravan in this valley. Therefore the traces of the people of 'Ad have not appeared until now, for they are buried over great distances beneath the sands.

Likewise, ancient remains everywhere are found only beneath the earth in excavations, because the agents of erosion bury them. So you find one of us, if he travels, for example, and leaves his house for several months, returning to find it covered with a layer of dust, even though it is tightly locked. So what about the open wilderness with the blowing of winds and hurricanes?

In Surat al-Fajr, the Truthful, glorified is He, gives us a glimpse of the history of these nations and what punishment befell them: ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with 'Ad, of Iram, of the pillars, the like of which was not created in the lands, and Thamud, who carved out the rocks in the valley, and Pharaoh, owner of the stakes, who transgressed in the lands and increased therein corruption? So your Lord poured upon them a scourge of punishment. Indeed, your Lord is ever watchful.﴾ [al-Fajr: 6-14].

Until now we do not know where their dwellings are, nor do we know their traces except what Allah has informed us of, because they are beneath great distances in the depths of the earth.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and warners had passed on before him and after him...﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 21]. He was not the first messenger to them, nor is he their last. The messengers passed ﴿before him...﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 21], that is, before him, ﴿and after him...﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 21], that is, after him.

The nudhur (warners) is the plural of nadhir, the one who frightens you and warns you of evil before it befalls you. The benefit of warning is that it alerts you to danger before you fall into it so that you avoid it, and the warning must come before the evil occurs by a sufficient period that enables you to remedy the matter and avoid falling into it.

As for His saying: ﴿that you worship none but Allah...﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 21], that is: this matter is one upon which all the messengers agreed, both those before Hud and those after him. All religions came only to serve this matter and to call people to it.

Worship, as we have explained, is the obedience of the worshipper to the commands and prohibitions of the one worshipped. This meaning nullifies and invalidates the worship of other than Allah, for they are all false gods and their worship is false, because they are gods without a method, without command and without prohibition.

So the sun: what did it say to the one who worshipped it? What did it command him and what did it forbid? What reward did it prepare for the one who worshipped it, and what did it prepare for the one who disbelieved in it? If you ask why people worshipped it and worshipped other things...

We say: because religiosity is an innate disposition in man since Allah created him and since he was in the world of souls. But true religion has demands and responsibilities that restrain the soul's rush and constrain its desires.

Therefore some resorted to a worship that satisfies their innate religiosity and releases them from the demands of true religion, so they turned to false gods and worshipped them, because they do not obligate them to anything and do not burden them with anything, and they unleash their desires.

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, I fear for you the punishment of a tremendous day﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 21]. This fear is the requirement of brotherhood, for the brother is eager for the welfare of his brother and eager for his salvation. Therefore Allah said regarding our master, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): ﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves; grievous to him is what you suffer, desirous of your welfare, to the believers kind and merciful﴾ [al-Tawbah: 128].

Here the day of punishment is described as a tremendous day. You in your worldly life describe some things as great, but this greatness in your material existence is subject to extinction, however long its term. Likewise every bliss in this world is spoiled for its possessor by two things: that the bliss escapes him, or that he escapes it and leaves it through death. So the description of this day as tremendous is because it is lasting and does not cease, and its possessor does not die so that he may rest from it.

The discussion here concerns the people of Hud. When he invited them to worship God alone, ﴿They said: "Have you come to us to turn us away⁠ ⁠from our gods..."﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 22], meaning: to turn us aside. "Our gods" means those that are claimed (to be gods). Al-ifk (turning away, falsehood) is turning a thing upside down from its proper state, diverting the truth into falsehood and the true into the false.

From this is His saying: ﴿And the overturned cities He hurled down⁠⁠﴾ [al-Najm: 53], which are the towns that God turned upside down. ﴿So bring us what you threaten us with...﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 22], meaning: the punishment, ﴿if you are of the truthful⁠⁠﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 22]. The punishment with which he threatened them did not come to them immediately; it will come on the Day of Resurrection, but they were hastening it.

Therefore He addressed them saying: ﴿Is it only now, when it has befallen you, that you believe in it, though you used to seek to hasten it?⁠⁠﴾ [Yunus: 51], and He said: ﴿The Day they will be tormented over the Fire. "Taste your trial; this is what you used to seek to hasten."⁠⁠﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 13-14].

So they sought to hasten the punishment because they did not believe in it and denied it, and had they believed in it, they would not have sought to hasten it.

Then he answers them with the natural reply:

﴿He said: "Knowledge of it is only with God..."⁠⁠﴾.

Its meaning: the knowledge of the Hour is with God. ﴿None will reveal its time except Him﴾ [al-A'raf: 187]. And I am only a messenger, conveying to you what I have been sent with from my Lord. ﴿But I see you to be a people acting ignorantly﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 23].

This is the essence of the matter: you are ignorant. That is, you have ignorance of affairs, and ignorance (jahl) is the great problem that confronts the messengers. Some understand that ignorance (jahl) is the absence of knowledge, but ignorance is a form of knowledge that contradicts the truth.

Therefore we have said: the unlettered person (ummi) who knows nothing and has no position is easier than the ignorant person, because his mind is empty, so you cast information to him and he accepts it. As for the ignorant person, he holds a position that contradicts the truth, so he needs to have it removed first, and so calling him to the truth is harder.

As for His saying: ﴿and I convey to you what I have been sent with﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 23], that is: I did not come of my own accord; rather I was brought to call you to God, so the act must be attributed to its doer. ﴿I have been sent﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 23], that is, by God, as we said regarding ﴿Glory be to the One who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque﴾ [al-Isra': 1]. Muhammad (ﷺ) did not say "I travelled," but said: "I was taken by night" (usriya bi).

This means that they are liars in their saying ﴿Have you come to us?﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 22], for he did not come of his own accord; rather God sent him to deliver the message. ﴿And upon the Messenger is only the clear conveyance﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 18]. So I am sent only to convey, and I do not know when the punishment will come; only the One who has power over it knows it.

﴿But I see you to be a people acting ignorantly﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 23], that is: you are ignorant that the Messenger came only as a conveyer, and that he has no knowledge of the descent of punishment upon those who denied him.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 46, verse 24:

That is: after they had hastened the punishment and said, ﴿So bring us what you threaten us with, if you are among the truthful﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 22], the punishment came to them in the form of a cloud. ﴿So when they saw it as a cloud spreading across their valleys…﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 24]. That is: a cloud crossing the expanse of the sky. ﴿Advancing toward their valleys…﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 24], coming towards them. ﴿They said, "This is a cloud bringing us rain…"﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 24]. That is: they took it to be an ordinary cloud that would rain on their valleys and bring them good.

So: the pronoun in ﴿saw it﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 24] refers to the cloud, because it is what is known from the context, as is shown by their saying "bringing us rain," since only a cloud rains. The indication (qarina) shows that it is the cloud.

The Qur'an often relies in its style on indications that clarify the referent of a pronoun, on the basis that the intellect grasps the matter by itself.

Recite: ﴿And if God were to take people to account for what they earned, He would not leave upon its back a single creature…﴾ [Fatir: 45]. What is meant is the surface of the earth, even though it is not mentioned in the context; but it comes to mind, and nothing else is understood from the speech.

The rule, then, is that a pronoun must have a referent, and there is no unspecified pronoun without a referent except one case: when the pronoun refers to the Absolute Unseen, namely the Truth, glorified and exalted be He. They cite His saying, ﴿Say: He is God, the One﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 1]. Who is "He"? God, because it can refer to none other than Him, glorified be He.

You say: "Zayd came, so I honoured him," meaning "I honoured Zayd." "Fatima came, so I honoured her," the pronoun referring to Fatima, and so on. The referent of a pronoun may be the very same thing, as when you say, "A man came to me, so I honoured him," meaning "I honoured the man." It may also refer to something other than the very same thing, as when you say, "I gave in charity a dirham and its half." The pronoun in "its half" does not refer to the dirham mentioned, but to a dirham like it, i.e., to half a dirham like it.

But why did they think the cloud crossing the sky would bring rain? They say: because they were in drought and famine, awaiting water, and they saw a cloud crossing the horizon of the sky, dark and slow in its movement, and these are the signs of a rain-bearing cloud, for the slowest of buckets is the fullest when filled, and the heaviest clouds in their motion are the most laden. So the slowness of the cloud is an indication that it is loaded with water, and since they were looking forward to rain, they took it to be rain.

So: it gave them hope of rain's descent, every sign pointed to it, and then suddenly this hope was cut off from them. Between the spreading of the soul by hope and its crushing by the severing of hope there is a kind of torment and grief, which they call "despair after longing" (yaʾs baʿd ṭamaʿ).

This is itself a form of torture, used for instance by those who run prisons: they withhold water from the prisoner until his thirst grows intense and he begs for it to drink. Then a soldier brings him a cup and brings it close to his lips, and then he throws it on the ground. This is pain and torment. Would that it had never been brought at all, for water brought before him is a trial above the trial of thirst.

Likewise the case of these people: they looked forward to rain and said, "It will rescue us from what we are in of drought." But instead, it sends down upon them the punishment in place of water. Behold, it is the punishment they had previously denied and hastened, ﴿Rather, it is what you hastened for: a wind in which is a painful punishment﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 24]. That is: the punishment that came in the form of ﴿a wind in which is a painful punishment﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 24].

We have said that the word "wind" (rīḥ), when it comes in the singular like this, indicates that it carries punishment and evil. So his saying "wind" means a general punishment, which is then detailed by ﴿in which is a painful punishment﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 24]. But when it comes in the plural ("winds," riyāḥ), it indicates good, as in His saying, ﴿and the turning of the winds…﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 5], because their turning drives the clouds, runs the ships, fertilises the flowers, etc.

Therefore the noble hadith reported regarding the supplication at the blowing of the wind [is well known]. It has already been explained that winds are an energy and a power that benefit and improve when they come from all directions, and destroy when they come from a single direction. The evacuation of air is now a science with rules that they use for destruction.

Moreover, air itself is one of the constituents of life, and without it there is no life. Therefore God made it a common, shared thing in the universe that no one owns, as they own food for example, for if the owner of the air withheld it from you for a moment you would die, unlike water and food, for example.

Then, after that, he elaborates on the phrase ﴿in which is a painful punishment﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 24], saying:

﴿It destroys everything by the command of its Lord…﴾.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 46, verse 25:

The word ﴿tudammiru﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 25] means "destroys." ﴿kulla shay'in﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 25] means "everything," i.e., it leaves nothing for them. ﴿bi-amri rabbihā﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 25] means "by the command of its Lord," its Creator and the One who sets it in motion. So it does not destroy by its own nature; rather, by God's command to it. Instead of bringing them good, it brought them evil. Here it needed an additional command from God to turn into evil and destroy rather than build up.

Only God possesses this command, and none but its Creator, glory be to Him, takes it out of its nature, just as He took the fire out of its nature in the story of our master Abraham, when He said to it: ﴿O fire, be coolness and safety upon Abraham﴾ [al-Anbiya: 69].

So: the wind responded to the command of its Lord, and it destroyed them with a destruction that left them nothing of their property except the remains of their houses. ﴿So they became such that none could be seen except their dwellings﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 25]. Why did it spare their dwellings?

They said: so that they would be a lesson for others, and a sign of their remains indicating them and the descent of punishment upon them, even though these settlements were buried under the earth. As we said, they were in a valley of sand called (al-Ahqaf), and it was this sand that buried them.

They said: when God willed to destroy them and sent against them the violent wind, the first among them to see the punishment was a woman who saw her house flying in the air like a bird.

When the punishment overtook them, they entered their houses seeking shelter from the severity of the gusts, but the wind entered the houses behind them, and the sand entered upon them until it buried them in it. The same wind that buried them is what uncovered them and exposed their corpses so that people might take heed from them, and then they were cast into the sea.

﴿Thus﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 25], i.e., in this manner, ﴿We recompense the guilty people﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 25]. So the recompense is neither injustice nor aggression; it is a requital of the same kind as the deed. They deserved this punishment only because they were guilty.

As for those who believed in our master Hud and affirmed his call, He protected them from the punishment by drawing a line around their dwellings, as if the state of their condition were saying: "O Lord, these are the believers in my call, so save them and guard them," and God saved them.

God's words ﴿Thus We recompense the guilty people﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 25] are a warning and admonition to the disbelievers of Quraysh. That is: O disbelievers of Quraysh, take a lesson from those who denied the messengers before you. This is the recompense of every disbeliever who opposes God's way and denies His messengers, and this is the picture before you.

Then the address turns to them:

﴿And We had established them in that wherein We have not established you...﴾.

This is an address to the Quraysh and a reminder to them that these people who were punished, the people of 'Ad, were stronger than you, had finer furnishings and appearance, and had more wealth than you. They tilled the earth and built it up, and they had a civilization among the greatest civilizations of the world. ﴿Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with 'Ad, Iram of the pillars, the like of which was never created in the lands?﴾ [Al-Fajr: 6-8].

Yet this was their fate. Their strength did not avail them, and their civilization did not ward off any of God's punishment. You are not stronger than they were. So beware of what they fell into by denying the Messenger, and beware lest there befall you what befell them.

As for His saying, ﴿And We had established them...﴾ [Al-Ahqaf: 26], it means: We established the people of 'Ad. Tamkin (establishment, empowerment) means: We gave them strength and capability, and We expanded for them the means of worldly life, so that they did what no other nation had done.

As for ﴿in that wherein We had not established you...﴾ [Al-Ahqaf: 26], the particle in here (in) is negative, as in His saying: ﴿Their mothers are not but those who bore them﴾ [Al-Mujadila: 2]. That is, their mothers are none but those who bore them. Here it means: We established for them what We did not establish for you, and We expanded for them means that We did not expand for you.

Then: ﴿And We gave them hearing and sight and hearts, but their hearing and their sight and their hearts availed them naught at all...﴾ [Al-Ahqaf: 26].

Hearing, sight and hearts are the principal means of human perception. In the Qur'an they always appear in this form: the word for hearing is singular, while the words for sight and hearts are plural.

This is one of the fine points of Qur'anic expression. Hearing is not made plural, because sound is heard by everyone in the same way; one hears the sound whether or not one sees its source. Sight, however, differs from person to person. One sees and another does not; one has sharp vision, another weak vision, and another is blind in one eye. Thus sights differ, and likewise hearts differ in receiving things.

It is established in the science of physiology that the ear is the first organ to function in the infant immediately after birth, while the eye sees after three to ten days, and after that the heart begins to function.

So this is the natural order in which the organs of perception function. Because of the importance of hearing, God made it the first of these organs to act. It is the first thing to receive perceptions after birth, and it is the sense whose task does not cease even in sleep.

The eye, for example, does not see during sleep, but the ear hears, because it is the means of rousing the sleeper. It must therefore always be ready to receive and listen.

We saw this matter in the story of the People of the Cave in His saying: ﴿So We struck upon their ears in the cave for a number of years﴾ [Al-Kahf: 11]. The cave lies in a desert where disturbing sounds are frequent at night, in addition to the sounds of thunder, lightning and wind. Had the ear remained in its natural state, these sounds would have disturbed them, but God struck upon their ears so that they would not hear.

Because hearing is the means of receiving and of conveying the message from God, God, glorified is He, made it the first of these faculties to act. For this reason our master, the Messenger of God (ﷺ), prescribed that we call the adhan (call to prayer) into the ear of the infant as soon as it is born.

If the ear did not function at that time, then taklif (moral responsibility) would be pointless. If you say, for example: Does the infant understand this? We say: Yes, it understands by means of the covenant that was taken from Adam when we were in the stage of the dhar (the primordial state of souls).

So the first thing parents must care for is to have the infant hear this call: God is greatest, God is greatest. This comes before everything else, and it is the faith-leaven around which all the leavens of faith revolve.

You still remember our discussion of His saying: ﴿And he who said to his parents, "Uff to you both!"...﴾ [Al-Ahqaf: 17]. What occupies these two parents at this stage of their son's life? They are not occupied with admission, then secondary school, then university. No, they are occupied with the more pressing and important matter, which is religion and creed. This deserves attention in childhood so that the child grows up upon it.

Therefore we greet the newborn with the words of the adhan, so that we plant them in him and in his make-up while he is pure of mind and clean of heart, so that they take firm root in him and are not separated from him, in accordance with the saying of the poet:

Her passion came to me before I knew passion,
and found a heart empty, so it settled firmly.

We said that hearing precedes sight in this world. In the Hereafter, however, they said: ﴿We have seen and we have heard...﴾ [As-Sajdah: 12]. Here sight precedes hearing, because when the Resurrection occurs, man is confronted with a dreadful scene, so he sees before he hears.

Then He says, describing the people of 'Ad: ﴿So their hearing availed them naught, nor their sight, nor their hearts, in anything...﴾ [Al-Ahqaf: 26]. That is, they heard as though they had not heard, and they saw as though they had not seen. They did not benefit from this, as He says: ﴿And We have placed veils over their hearts, lest they understand it, and in their ears a deafness...﴾ [Al-Isra: 46].

Consequently their hearts became empty, as He, glorified is He, says: ﴿And their hearts are void﴾ [Ibrahim: 43].

And He says: ﴿And We have certainly created for Hell many of the jinn and mankind. They have hearts with which they do not understand, they have eyes with which they do not see, and they have ears with which they do not hear. Those are like livestock; rather, they are further astray. Those are the heedless﴾ [Al-A'raf: 179].

But what is the relationship between hearing, sight and the heart, that is, the mind? And why did He combine them? They said: Because hearing perceives what is heard, and sight perceives what is seen. From these perceptions man forms thought, then presents it to the intellect so that it may choose from it and distinguish among its components. So he takes the good and leaves the bad, takes the right and leaves the wrong, takes what agrees with the Shari'ah and leaves what contradicts it.

When he settles upon a matter, he casts it into the heart so that it may be fixed there as a firm creed that does not waver, and a faith that does not fluctuate or rise again to the intellect to be debated once more. Thus the heart is the seat of beliefs.

For this reason our master, the Messenger of God (ﷺ), said of it: [the heart is the vessel that carries the fluid of life and pumps it to all parts of the body]. When it is filled with faith, it pumps this faith with the blood to all parts of the body, so that actions and deeds come into line with this faith, and each sense performs its task precisely.

Thus you find that the Giver of life does not give you that which hinders you from Him, nor that which obstructs the performance of His method. Therefore read: ﴿And when they hear idle talk, they turn away from it and say, "To us our deeds, and to you your deeds. Peace be upon you; we do not seek the ignorant."﴾ [Al-Qasas: 55].

And He says: ﴿And it has already been revealed to you in the Book that when you hear the verses of God being denied and mocked, do not sit with them until they enter into a conversation other than that. Indeed, in that case, you would be like them. Indeed, God will gather the hypocrites and the disbelievers in Hell all together﴾ [An-Nisa: 140].

So when faith takes root in the heart of the servant, nothing issues from him except what agrees with the requirements of faith, in speech and in action, and all his movements in life are stamped with this character. As for the people of 'Ad of whom we speak, they did not benefit from what they heard from their Messenger, nor from what they saw of the signs of the universe. Therefore they did not taste the sweetness of faith in God.

﴿Because they used to deny the signs of God...﴾ [Al-Ahqaf: 26], rejecting them and turning away from them. Had they believed, God would have expanded their breasts. But God set a seal upon their hearts, upon their hearing, and upon their sight, because they chose disbelief and loved it, so God aided them in it, for He is a Lord who gives His servant what he wants.

For this reason we said to a woman who exaggerates her grief over the loss of someone dear to her: Beware of that. Step out of the circle of grief and do not become attached to it. Look not at what was taken but at what remains; otherwise God will perpetuate your grief and take away what remains to you.

Here is an important lesson: if some harm befalls you in something dear to you, do not look at what the calamity has taken, but look at what it has left you, so that it may be easier for you, and so that you do not enter through the door of despair and hopelessness. You will find that what remains is greater, and that your calamity is lighter than that of others.

For this reason, when people came to the wise man of China complaining to him of the troubles and worries of life, he said to them: Let each of you write his worries and troubles on a piece of paper, then cast it into this box, and come to me after a week. After a week the complainers came, and he said to the first: Put your hand in and take a paper from what is in the box. He took a paper.

When he looked at it, he said: I do not want my paper. Why? Because he found that his calamity was lighter than the calamity of another. The common people have rendered this meaning in their saying: "Whoever sees the troubles of people, his own trouble becomes easy for him."

It is related that our master 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr travelled to the Umayyad caliph in Syria. On the way his leg was injured, and he found no one to treat it until he reached Damascus. There they found that it had become gangrenous, and they found no solution but to amputate it. They searched for an anaesthetic for him, meaning "bang" [a narcotic], but he said: No, for I do not like to be heedless of my Lord for the blink of an eye. But leave me until I enter into the prayer.

When he entered his prayer, they amputated his leg, and he did not feel it. Then they took it, wrapped it in a shroud, and he said to them: Give it to me. He held it and said: "O God, if You have tried me in one limb, You have granted me well-being in other limbs."

Yes. Does one who is absorbed in the presence of God feel pain? We must believe these reports and not deem them unlikely, for it is one of the secrets of the ear that when you seal it completely, you do not feel pain. If you try and feel some pain, know that you have not sealed it completely.

The call "God is greatest" is what takes you out of worldly activity and places you before God. It is the takbir al-ihram (opening takbir) for entering the prayer. We have previously explained that the meaning of "God is greatest" is that work and striving are considered great, but God is greater. Therefore worldly work, striving in it, and drawing out its good things must never be belittled. This world is too important to be forgotten, but it is too lowly to be an ultimate goal.

Whoever follows the story of the people of 'Ad finds that it is mentioned in several surahs. It is mentioned here in summary and brevity, and the detailed account of this story comes in Surah Hud.

In Surah Al-Haqqah, the scene of punishment mentioned here is detailed. He, glorified is He, says: ﴿As for 'Ad, they were destroyed by a furious, violent wind. He imposed it upon them for seven nights and eight days in succession, so you could see the people lying prostrate as though they were trunks of hollow palm trees. So do you see any remnant of them?﴾ [Al-Haqqah: 6-8].

The wind that destroyed them was a sarsar wind, meaning: fierce, with a disturbing sound, coming upon them from above, for seven nights and eight days, ḥusūman. Ḥusūm is the plural of ḥāsim, so it is decisive: it settled the matter and ended the affair, leaving them nothing.

If you say: why does He say ﴿seven nights and eight days﴾ [Al-Haqqah: 7], when the custom in legislation is that nights precede days, and time enters with its night rather than its day? The proof is that we establish the entry of Ramadan by its night, for before we fast we pray the night prayer.

For this reason they made it a jurisprudential riddle: which period precedes the obligation? It seems that the punishment came upon them in the morning, so it began with the day and ended at sunset, and thus it lasted seven nights and eight days.

The orientalists have stopped at this verse, objecting to the Qur'anic manner of making the number feminine with a masculine noun and masculine with a feminine noun: ﴿seven nights and eight days﴾ [Al-Haqqah: 7]. They said: When do men wear women's necklaces, and when do mistresses of the curtained chambers appear in men's turbans?

The rule in grammar is that the numbers from three to nine are opposite to the counted noun in gender, and there is a reason for this. The original form of a word is masculine. You say (kātib, writer, masculine). The feminine needs a marker to distinguish it, so they placed the feminine marker ta' marbuta and you say (kātiba, writer, feminine).

Thus the feminine is a branch of the masculine, so it needs something to distinguish it. As for the number words from three to nine, they are originally formed on the feminine: you say thalāthah, arba'ah, khamsah.

So when they come with a masculine noun, they remain in their original form, and with a feminine noun they need a marker. Instead of bringing another marker, they removed the marker found in the feminine.

Thus the number came in contrast to the counted noun in gender, and He says: ﴿seven nights and eight days﴾ [Al-Haqqah: 7].

Furthermore, according to astronomers, a day is reckoned from one moment to the same moment on the following day. Therefore, at one o'clock in the afternoon they say: "one p.m.," while we are still in the middle of the day. Likewise at one o'clock after midnight they say: "one a.m.," while we are still in the night. But in legislation, the day is from sunrise to sunset, and the night is from sunset to sunrise.

We note that this surah contains some scenes of the story, but a detailed account is in a surah named after it, the surah of (Hud), which deals with many scenes not mentioned here.

In this surah the context focuses on three scenes or matters: the call to worship God alone, then the warning against worshipping other than Him, because if they worship other than God they expose themselves to punishment, and he is their brother who is keen for their salvation. Then they answered him: ﴿Have you come to us to turn us away from our gods? So bring us what you threaten us with, if you are of the truthful﴾ [Al-Ahqaf: 22].

As for Surah Hud, it added other scenes. There He says: ﴿And to 'Ad, their brother Hud. He said, "O my people, worship God; you have no deity other than Him..."﴾ [Hud: 50]. This agrees with what is here. Here He said: ﴿I fear for you the punishment of a great day﴾ [Al-A'raf: 59], and there He said: ﴿You are not but fabricators﴾ [Hud: 50]. Fabrication gives rise to great punishment.

Thus, here He speaks of the cause and there of the means. The great punishment has as its cause that you fabricated against God by taking partners for Him.

Then Hud adds another point, His saying: ﴿O my people, I do not ask you for any payment for it. My payment is only from the One who created me. Then will you not reason?﴾ [Hud: 51].

It is as if the matter is one of reason and the law of exchange: that I deserve a wage for my call to you. But I do not want any payment from you, for you cannot provide it, since it is great and beyond your capacity. Therefore I seek it only from God, who sent me and appointed me for this task.

His saying ﴿He who created me﴾ [Hud: 51] means: who brought me into being and produced me. He did not say "who sent me," for the meaning is that He created me to be a messenger, fit to carry His call, and to be His envoy to His creation.

Even his name came in agreement with this mission, for the word Hud comes from hāda, meaning: he returned, repented and turned back to his Lord. From it comes His saying: ﴿Indeed, we have turned back to You﴾ [Al-A'raf: 156], meaning: we repented and returned to God.

Then in Hud, he commands them to seek forgiveness and repent: ﴿And O my people, ask forgiveness of your Lord and then repent to Him...﴾ [Hud: 52]. Seeking forgiveness is for a sin that has passed, while repentance is not returning to sin again, so it concerns the future. Then he explains to them the fruit of this: ﴿He will send the sky upon you in abundant rain and will increase you in strength to your strength, and do not turn away as criminals﴾ [Hud: 52]. This is not mentioned in Al-Ahqaf.

Among the details found in (Hud) but not mentioned here is their saying: ﴿We only say that some of our gods have struck you with evil.﴾ He said: ﴿Indeed, I call Allah to witness, and bear witness yourselves that I am free from what you associate.﴾ [Hud: 54].

Here we note that he did not lay claim to the charge for himself, but returned it to Allah. He disavows this statement, then says to them: ﴿Indeed, I have put my trust in Allah, my Lord and your Lord. There is no creature but that He holds its forelock. Indeed, my Lord is on a straight path.﴾ [Hud: 56].

The trust of the believer in his Lord appears in his speech here. He says, challenging them: Do whatever you wish. I did not come to you of my own accord, nor do I confront you with my status, my strength, or my kinsmen. Rather, I confront you with Allah, who sent me, and in whom I have placed my trust in my call.

Here is an important doctrinal lesson: when calamity befalls you, do not despair and do not rage, but return to the reserve of faith within yourself. If your means fail, the laws of Allah do not fail; if the causes forsake you, the Causer exists, so return to Him.

In (Hud) there is also a scene of the salvation of those who believed in him, not mentioned here: ﴿And when Our command came, We saved Hud and those who believed with him by mercy from Us, and We saved them from a severe punishment.﴾ [Hud: 58]. This is a cosmic sign that broke all the laws of nature: ﴿And when Our command came...﴾ [Hud: 58], meaning, by their destruction and the punishment they had been hastening, We saved Hud and those who believed with him. By what? ﴿By mercy from Us...﴾ [Hud: 58]. Only the mercy of Allah overtook them, because what happened was a natural upheaval and an outburst of nature against those who opposed the Creator of this nature. The wind was the wind: a violent, destructive, disturbing storm, a fierce, roaring gale. Yet it defied all the laws of environmental formation: it destroyed these people and spared those.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 46, verse 27:

The address here is to the Quraysh, wishing to draw their attention to the fate of the nations that denied (the messengers) around them. ﴿And [We destroyed] what is around you of the towns⟩ [al-Ahqaf: 27], meaning: around Makkah.

He addressed them elsewhere: ﴿And indeed you pass by them in the morning, and at night. Will you not then reason?⟩ [al-Saffat: 137-138]. Yes, they pass by the cities of Salih, by the people of Nuh, and by al-Ahqaf, (the dwelling place) of 'Ad and Thamud, and they see their traces and what overtook them of the punishment of Allah.

And in another place He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its outlying parts? And Allah judges; there is no repeller of His judgment, and He is swift in reckoning⟩ [al-Ra'd: 41].

Meaning: O Quraysh, be alert and do not be deceived by what you have of sovereignty over the Arabs and control over the tribes of the Arabian Peninsula, and that you have a standing in the hearts of people, for the power of faith that penetrates the hearts of people will pull the carpet of sovereignty from under your feet.

And here you are, seeing every day the increase of the land of faith and the shrinking of the area of disbelief, so take a lesson from that. This matter was the cause of the faith of Khalid ibn al-Walid, 'Amr ibn al-'As, and others from the leaders and chiefs of disbelief, when they saw that the affair of Muhammad was increasing, so they said: "The affair of Muhammad has become manifest and firm, and he has acquired a power that no one can stand against," and indeed they believed in his call.

As for His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿And We have varied the signs...⟩ [al-Ahqaf: 27], meaning: We turned them and displayed the proofs for them in every aspect and by various methods: ﴿that they might return⟩ [al-Ahqaf: 27], meaning: from their pride, arrogance and obstinacy, that they might return from their disbelief and denial of the blessings of Allah. For after they had received the blessing, they disbelieved in the Benefactor and set up partners for Him.

Therefore, in the verse after it He said:

﴿Why then did those they had taken as gods besides Allah not help them?...⟩ [al-Ahqaf: 28].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 46, verse 28:

Meaning: These are the deities they took besides Allah. ﴿Why then...﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 28]. Meaning: "Why not" (halla); it expresses urging, and in meaning it is a mockery of them, i.e., why did they not help them and stand by their side in their calamities? And the meaning of ﴿as an offering...﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 28] is: means of drawing them near to Allah. All of this did not happen. Why? Because they are false, claimed deities, which neither harm nor benefit.

Rather, they are the product of their own hands. They themselves undertook their fashioning: they set up the stone and gave it two arms, two legs, a nose and an ear. When it fell, they lifted it up; when its arm was broken, they repaired it. By Allah, are these minds?

Their saying ﴿as an offering...﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 28] is like what they said in another place: ﴿We only worship them so that they may bring us near to Allah in nearness﴾ [al-Zumar: 3].

It is strange of them to say this, for they are the people of eloquence and clear expression, and they know well the meaning of worship. If they had said, "We only honor them so that they bring us near to Allah," it would have been reasonable. But ﴿worship them...﴾ [al-Zumar: 3], and you know that worship is obedience to the command of the one worshipped in his commands and prohibitions. Do these deities have any commands or prohibitions?

Therefore Allah responds to them: ﴿Rather, they went astray from them...﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 28]. Meaning: they became lost and vanished from them, from our saying "so-and-so lost the way" (ḍalla). And among it is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And when harm touches you at sea, those whom you call upon vanish except Him...﴾ [al-Isra: 67]. Why? Because the matter is destruction.

A person does not deceive himself. In a time of hardship he abandons the claimed deities and turns to the true God, who possesses benefit and possesses harm. In such a situation he never says, "O Hubal," because he knows that Hubal will not save him; rather he says, "O Allah."

﴿And that...﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 28] refers to their taking deities besides Allah. ﴿Their falsehood...﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 28]. Ifk is deliberate lying, and it is the most severe kind of lying. ﴿And what they used to fabricate﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 28]: what they invented of falsehood, from their saying that these are deities. So the general meaning of the verse is: the absence of help is the result of falsehood and of fabricating against Allah by taking deities besides Him.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 46, verses 29–30:

The context shifts to another field of da'wah. Having told us about the stance of mankind, and how some of them affirmed the Messenger of Allah or denied him, he now speaks to us about the jinn, who are the counterpart of mankind in the call.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was sent to both the two weighty creations, mankind and the jinn. So the jinn are a race under obligation (mukallaf) like us, but they are unseen by us, so we do not see them: ﴿Indeed, he and his tribe see you from where you cannot see them...﴾ [al-A'raf: 27].

The jinn have lightness of movement and penetrate into things because of their fiery nature. So if fire were lit behind this wall, after a few moments you would feel it here. Therefore, believe that they are made of fire, that they penetrate through things, and that they have a nature different from the nature of the human being.

God, glorified is He, wants to make clear to us that the jinn, although they are absent from us, are like us in being under obligation, and like us they are addressed by the Qur'an, among them the believer and the disbeliever, the obedient and the disobedient.

We know the story of the conflict between the jinn and the human being, from the time God created Adam, peace be upon him, and commanded Iblis to prostrate to him, but he refused and was arrogant. His argument was that he was created from fire and Adam was created from clay, so how should he prostrate to one who is (in his view) inferior to him, in his words: ﴿You created me from fire and You created him from clay﴾ [al-A'raf: 12].

It is true that Adam too fell into disobedience, but there is a great difference between the disobedience of Adam and the disobedience of Iblis. Adam disobeyed his Lord when he ate from the tree which God had forbidden him to eat from; he disobeyed out of heedlessness, the overpowering of the self, and the whispering of Satan.

Then, when he recognised his disobedience, he acknowledged it, repented of it, and confessed that he had wronged his Lord and wronged himself: ﴿They said: "Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers"﴾ [al-A'raf: 23]. In al-Baqarah He said: ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words, and He accepted his repentance. Indeed, He is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 37].

So, the repentance of Adam was accepted because he did not reject the ruling of God. As for Iblis, he rejected the ruling and did not submit to it, so he was expelled from the mercy of God and removed. There is a difference between disobeying a ruling while you acknowledge it and believe it is from God, and rejecting it.

Therefore we say these words to one who argues, for example, about matters of religion whose ruling is clear, such as usury (riba) or letting the beard grow. He says: "Dealing in usury is now permissible." We say to him: by this statement you reject the ruling of God concerning usury. The safer course for you is to say that it is forbidden, but my circumstances compel me to it, for example.

Then you may follow your father Adam and repent. Seek forgiveness, perhaps God will forgive you, rather than opposing your Lord in His ruling. You cannot bear this. And remember the words of Satan: ﴿And I will surely command them, and they will change the creation of God...﴾ [al-Nisa': 119].

So beware of this matter. You know that Iblis was once, in his time, the "peacock of the angels" (Tawus al-Mala'ika). When he opposed, became arrogant, and rejected the ruling of God, He made him accursed and expelled from the mercy of God.

We have an important observation in God's command to Adam not to eat from the tree: ﴿And do not approach this tree...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 35]. The prohibition is against merely approaching it. And so it is with every command concerning what God has forbidden: ﴿These are the limits of God, so do not approach them...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187].

As for what God has made lawful for you, He said concerning it: ﴿These are the limits of God, so do not transgress them...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229], meaning: do not transgress what God has made lawful. As for the forbidden, do not even approach it, because whoever grazes around the protected pasture is about to fall into it.

The offspring of Iblis follow his course in misleading the children of Adam. We do not see them, just as we do not see the angels, with the difference between them: the angels are made of light, and the devils are made of fire.

Here the discourse moves from the message of Muhammad ﷺ to mankind to the jinn, and the report that the jinn are under obligation and that they listen to the Qur'an. Muhammad ﷺ did not bring this from himself; rather he relates to us what God informed him, that the jinn listen to the Qur'an.

So He said in the surah of the Jinn: ﴿Say: "It has been revealed to me that a group of the jinn listened and said: Indeed, we have heard a wondrous Qur'an, which guides to righteousness, so we have believed in it..."﴾ [al-Jinn: 1–2].

It is as if God, glorified is He, says to His Prophet Muhammad: I did not send you to go to the jinn and address them, because you do not see them. Therefore I turned them towards you and brought them to you so that they might listen to the Qur'an while you are unaware of them. Had I not informed you of that, you would not have known it.

Here He says: ﴿And [mention] when We turned to you a group of the jinn listening to the Qur'an...﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 29], so you recite while they listen around you.

Their words in the surah of the Jinn, ﴿which guides to righteousness...﴾ [al-Jinn: 2], and here they said: ﴿a Book revealed after Moses...﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 30], indicate that the jinn have a connection with the earlier prophets, and that they are under obligation like us.

In the surah of al-Rahman: ﴿We will soon attend to you, O two weighty ones﴾ [al-Rahman: 31], meaning: We will take account of you. After We left you at your ease to do what you wish, do not think that this is heedlessness on Our part concerning you. Rather, We gave you respite in order to affirm the matter of choice which We created in you and granted you.

So the two weighty creations, the jinn and mankind, are equal in reckoning, just as they are equal in obligation.

It was narrated from our master Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: I was with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on one of the mountains of Makkah, when there came toward us an old man with a staff he leaned upon. When the Messenger saw him, he recognised him, and said: "It is as if this is the gait of a jinni," and he composed (verses). The man said: "Yes, I am from the jinn." The Messenger said to him: "Who are you?" He said: "I am Hamah ibn Haym ibn Laqis ibn Iblis." He said to him: "Between you and your father Iblis are there two fathers?" He said: "Yes, and I have lived most of the age and a little remains. And I witnessed Qabil while he was killing Habil."

This report is evidence of the length of their lifespans and that they take on different forms, just as the angel does. We do not see the angel in his true form, nor do we see the jinni in his true form, except when he takes the form of a human being.

You know the long hadith of Gabriel. Therefore we see some enemies of the Muhammadan call raising certain difficulties around it, among them their saying that the Messenger should be an angel. This difficulty is rejected: if the Messenger had come as an angel, he would have come to them in the form of a man; otherwise, how would he convey to them, and how would the receiving from him take place?

So the difficulty remains. Moreover, an angel cannot be a valid model, because they do not disobey God in what He commands them, and they do what they are commanded. How could he be a model for one whose nature is error, heedlessness, and forgetfulness?

Therefore a condition for the prophet and messenger is that he be of the same kind as those to whom he is sent, so that the model may be realised in him.

God, glorified is He, has given us a detailed picture of the state of the jinn, that among them are believers and disbelievers. He said, relating about them: ﴿And among us are the Muslims, and among us are the deviators. Whoever embraces Islam, those have sought out the right course. But as for the deviators, they will be fuel for Hell﴾ [al-Jinn: 14–15].

Therefore the Prophet ﷺ said: [...], so to You is praise, they repeat it according to the repetition of the verse.

Listen to them saying: ﴿And that He, exalted is the majesty of our Lord...﴾ [al-Jinn: 3], meaning: His majesty is exalted, and because of this majesty ﴿He has not taken a companion or a son﴾ [al-Jinn: 3]. So the jinn know the matters of faith and the matters of tawhid, and perhaps they were more precise than us in expressing them. It is enough that they judged Iblis to be foolish, saying: ﴿And that our foolish one used to say about Allah an excessive transgression﴾ [al-Jinn: 4].

Let us return to what we were discussing from His saying: ﴿And [mention] when We turned to you a group of the jinn listening to the Qur'an...﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 29]. The nafar are the group from three to forty. "We turned them to you" means: We brought them to you instead of you going to them.

﴿So when they attended it...﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 29]: they attended the recitation. ﴿They said: "Listen attentively"...﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 29]: they listened with attention and reflection, meaning some of them instructed others to listen silently. ﴿So when it was concluded...﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 29]: the recitation ended. ﴿They turned back to their people as warners﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 29]: they went to their people to warn them and convey to them what they had heard.

﴿They said: "O our people, indeed we have heard a Book revealed after Moses..."﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 30], that is, the Qur'an. Their saying "after Moses" indicates that they had a connection with the earlier messengers, and that they were believers in our master Moses, meaning they were from the Jews.

They mentioned Moses without Jesus, peace be upon them both, because the Book of Moses is the method that organises the movement of life, and in it are laws and rulings, whereas the Book of Jesus was merely matters of feeling and admonitions. Therefore they paid attention to this matter and combined the Gospel and the Torah in one book, despite the partisanship between them, and they named it the Holy Book.

The meaning of ﴿confirming...﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 30] is that the Qur'an confirms ﴿what is before it...﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 30], the heavenly books that came before it. And since it confirms them, it came with what they came with, but it adds to them that it ﴿guides to the truth and to a straight path﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 30], in a manner suited to the universality of religion.

Every messenger before Muhammad came to treat the diseases of his society in a limited time and a limited place. Two messengers might be contemporaries, as we saw with our master Abraham: our master Lot was his contemporary, and our master Moses was contemporary with our master Shu'ayb.

The world at that time was in isolation and separation. There was not the connection that exists now, which makes the whole world like a small village. This isolated life made every society unaware of others.

Therefore each had its own particular corruptions, each of which needed a messenger to correct it and to take the hand of his people to God. Some people worshipped idols besides God, others cheated in measure and weight, and others deviated sexually from the nature God had created. Each of these groups needed a messenger.

But when the world became connected and means of travel came into existence, one messenger was necessary, because the corruptions and horizons would become unified. There had to be one messenger suitable for every time and every place. Therefore every time and every place was honoured by the one who gathers all good in every time and every place: Muhammad ibn Abdullah ﷺ.

So among the jinn there was a group who listened and undertook the duty of conveying the message. Therefore the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Yes. And who knows, perhaps the one who conveys may be more eager to apply it than the one who hears." The Arab poet was alert to this meaning and said:

So take from my knowledge and do not look at my deeds,
and pick the fruit and leave the branch to the fire.

Then this group of jinn continue to convey to their people and warn them with what they heard:

﴿O our people, respond to the caller of Allah...﴾.
